questions.question: Claude keeps adding a closing paragraph you do not want. What is the efficient instruction?
options: 'End after the final bullet; do not add a closing paragraph'
'Keep it brief and skip anything that is not essential'
'Rewrite this without the fluff at the end'
'Match the length of the previous version exactly'
questions.explanation: State the exact boundary. 'Without the fluff at the end' points at the problem but leaves Claude to decide what counts as fluff, so the closing often comes back shorter rather than gone.

questions.question: For a long, careful analysis of a 60-page report, which is the better choice?
options: The fastest model, since it can be run several times and the answers compared
The most capable model, accepting slower responses for the depth of analysis
A smaller model with the report split into chunks so each fits in a short prompt
Whichever model the team used last time, so results are comparable across reports
questions.explanation: Depth favors capability. Chunking the report for a smaller model is the strongest alternative, but it loses the cross-references between sections that a careful analysis depends on.

questions.question: Which feature lets a whole team share standing instructions and files?
options: A saved conversation that each team member opens and continues
A shared browser bookmark to a chat with the instructions pinned at the top
A shared Project with the instructions and files attached
A team email thread that holds the latest version of the instructions
questions.explanation: Projects share context. A saved conversation looks similar but mixes everyone's messages into one growing thread, and it has no place for instructions that apply to every new conversation.

questions.question: A colleague asks whether to use the consumer chat app or an organization workspace for client work. Deciding factor?
options: Data handling and admin controls: the organization workspace governs what happens to client data
Response speed and rate limits, since client work is time-sensitive and volume can be high
Which one has access to the newest model, since client deliverables should use the best output
Cost per seat, since the consumer app is cheaper and client budgets are tight
questions.explanation: Data handling and admin controls decide; client work belongs in the governed workspace. Model access is a real difference between plans, but a better model in an ungoverned account does not fix where the client's data goes.

questions.question: Which task fits Claude Code rather than the chat app?
options: Drafting a newsletter that goes out to the engineering team each month
Summarizing a recorded architecture review call for the people who missed it
Writing a job post for a senior developer role from the hiring manager's notes
Making the same change across dozens of files in a code repository
questions.explanation: Repository work is Claude Code's job. The other three are about engineers but are still drafting and summarizing tasks, which the chat app handles well; what matters is whether the work happens inside a codebase.

questions.question: When would a smaller, faster model be the right pick?
options: For legal or medical analysis, where a concise answer is safer than a long one
For high-volume, simple tasks like tagging or short drafts where speed and cost matter more than depth
When the team is new to AI tools, since simpler models are easier to prompt well
When the conversation is going to run long, since smaller models hold context more reliably over time
questions.explanation: Match model to task: volume and simplicity favor speed and cost. Legal and medical analysis is the trap, because concise is not the same as careful, and those are the tasks where depth matters most.

questions.question: What belongs in a Project's instructions?
options: Every document the team has produced on the topic, so Claude has the fullest possible picture
A log of past conversations that went well, so Claude can reproduce the pattern
Standing context: who the audience is, tone, formats, and rules that apply to every conversation
The specific request for this week, updated each time the task changes
questions.explanation: Standing rules, not everything. This week's request belongs in the conversation, not the instructions, because it changes; documents belong in knowledge files rather than instructions, and even then only the ones the project regularly needs.

questions.question: Your Project's knowledge files are out of date and answers reflect old policy. Fix?
options: Add the new policy document alongside the old ones so Claude can see both versions
Add a line to the instructions telling Claude to prefer the most recent file when they conflict
Start a new Project from scratch and move the team over once it is set up
Replace the outdated files and tell the team that the source of truth has changed
questions.explanation: Maintain the knowledge base: remove what is wrong and tell people. Keeping both versions with a 'prefer the newest' rule leaves the old policy available to be quoted, and Claude cannot reliably tell which file is newer from the content.

questions.question: What is a good way to keep a team's prompts consistent?
options: Shared templates or skills with the agreed structure, stored where the team can find them
One designated person who writes every prompt and sends it to the rest of the team
A weekly review where the team compares the prompts each person wrote that week
A rule that everyone uses the same model so the outputs come out in a similar style
questions.explanation: Shared, findable templates keep structure consistent without a bottleneck. A single prompt writer gives consistency but does not scale and stops the moment that person is away; a weekly review compares prompts after the inconsistent work is already done.

questions.question: Which is a reason to split work into several Projects?
options: The knowledge files are large and splitting them spreads the storage across Projects
Different audiences, tones, or confidentiality levels that should not mix
Projects perform better when each one holds fewer than ten conversations
Each team member should own a Project so their conversations stay private
questions.explanation: Separate contexts that should not blend. One Project per person is the common misuse: it splits by owner instead of by context, so the shared instructions and files that make a Project useful end up duplicated or missing.

questions.question: How much should a knowledge file contain?
options: Everything the team has written on the topic, so nothing relevant is left out
A single summary page, since longer files make answers slower and less focused
Only finalized documents; drafts and working notes should stay out of the Project
What conversations in that Project regularly need, kept current
questions.explanation: Relevant and current is the rule. 'Only finalized documents' sounds disciplined, but a current working draft is often exactly what conversations need; the test is whether the content is used and up to date, not its approval status.

questions.question: What should you record when a prompt template works well?
options: The template, the inputs it expects, and an example output, so others can reuse it
The model version and the date, so the team knows when it may need to be re-tested
The name of the person who wrote it, so colleagues know who to ask about it
The number of times it has been used, so the team can see which templates matter
questions.explanation: Document reusable assets so others can pick them up. Model version and date are worth noting alongside, but on their own they do not let anyone reuse the template; the inputs and an example output are what make it usable.

questions.question: Claude's answer ignores an attached document. First thing to check?
options: Whether the model you selected supports file attachments of that size and type
Whether the document contains text or only scanned images, which need conversion first
That the document uploaded correctly and that your prompt refers to it explicitly
Whether the conversation is too long and the document has dropped out of context
questions.explanation: Confirm the input and the reference before anything else. Scanned images and context length are real causes, but they are second-line checks; most cases are a failed upload or a prompt that never mentions the document.

questions.question: A conversation has drifted and answers are worse. What helps?
options: Ask Claude to summarize the conversation so far and continue from that summary in the same chat
Shorten your messages so the model has less new text to process each turn
Switch to a more capable model mid-conversation so it can recover the thread
Start a new conversation with a concise summary of the task and decisions so far
questions.explanation: Reset with a clean brief. Summarizing inside the same chat is the near miss: the summary helps, but the drifted history is still in the context and keeps pulling answers off course.

questions.question: Claude says it cannot access a link you pasted. Why?
options: The link is too long for the model to parse; shorten it with a URL shortener and try again
It may not be able to browse, or the page may be restricted; paste the content instead
The page needs a login; sign in yourself first and paste the link again, since the session carries over
The link is broken; check it in your browser and resend it once it loads
questions.explanation: Provide the content directly. Signing in yourself does nothing, because your browser session does not carry over to the model; if the page is behind a login or the model cannot browse, pasting the text is the only reliable route.

questions.question: Output is in the wrong format despite instructions. Fastest fix?
options: Repeat the same instruction more firmly and put it at the very end of the prompt
Switch to a more capable model, since format compliance improves with model size
Show a short example of the exact format you want
Ask Claude to explain why it chose that format before trying again
questions.explanation: Examples fix format faster than any description. Repeating the instruction more firmly sometimes works, but an example removes the ambiguity that caused the miss in the first place.
